**Answer Explanation**

For the set of \(S\)-smooth numbers we write each element uniquely as  

\[
n = p_1^{a_1}\,p_2^{a_2}\dots p_r^{a_r},\qquad a_i\ge 0 .
\]

Thus an element corresponds to a lattice point \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots ,a_r)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^r\).
For a fixed \(\mathbf a\) the forbidden configuration  

\[
\{n,\;p_1n,\dots ,p_rn\}
\]

is exactly the set of points  

\[
\{\mathbf a,\;\mathbf a+e_1,\dots ,\mathbf a+e_r\},
\]

where \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th unit vector.  
Hence every “hyper‑edge’’ contains \(r+1\) points, one with total exponent  

\[
s=\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_i,
\]

and the other \(r\) points with total exponent \(s+1\).

---

### A construction attaining density \(\frac{r}{r+1}\)

Colour each lattice point by the residue of its total exponent modulo \(r+1\):

\[
\chi(\mathbf a)=\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_i\Bigr)\bmod (r+1)\in\{0,1,\dots ,r\}.
\]

For any edge \(\{\mathbf a,\mathbf a+e_1,\dots ,\mathbf a+e_r\}\) we have  

\[
\chi(\mathbf a)=c,\qquad 
\chi(\mathbf a+e_i)=c+1\pmod{r+1}\quad\text{for all }i .
\]

Thus the edge uses exactly two colours, one appearing once (the base) and the other \(r\) times.
If we delete **all** points of a single colour (say colour \(k\)) and keep the remaining \(r\) colours, every edge loses at least one of its vertices: either its base (when \(\chi(\mathbf a)=k\)) or all its “upper’’ vertices (when \(\chi(\mathbf a+e_i)=k\)).  
Consequently we obtain a subset of \(M(S)\cap[1,X]\) with size

\[
\frac{r}{r+1}\,\Psi_S(X)+o(\Psi_S(X)).
\]

Hence  

\[
\liminf_{X\to\infty}\frac{F_S(X)}{\Psi_S(X)}\ge\frac{r}{r+1}.
\]

---

### Upper bound

Consider the hypergraph whose vertices are the \(S\)-smooth numbers \(\le X\) and whose hyper‑edges are exactly the forbidden \((r+1)\)-tuples.  
Every vertex belongs to many edges, and each edge has size \(r+1\).  
A standard fractional‑cover argument (or simply averaging over all edges) shows that any subset avoiding a full edge must miss at least a fraction \(1/(r+1)\) of the vertices; otherwise the average number of kept vertices per edge would exceed \(r\), contradicting the definition of a forbidden edge. Formally,

\[
\frac{F_S(X)}{\Psi_S(X)}\le 1-\frac{1}{r+1} = \frac{r}{r+1}.
\]

---

### Limit value

The lower and upper bounds coincide, so the limit exists and equals the common value:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{F_S(X)}{\Psi_S(X)}=\frac{r}{r+1}}.
\]

Thus the asymptotic maximal proportion of \(S\)-smooth numbers that can be selected while avoiding any full set \(\{n,p_1n,\dots ,p_rn\}\) depends only on the number \(r\) of primes in \(S\) and is \(r/(r+1)\).

**ANSWER:** r/(r+1)
